title: Larry's on Vacation

jokes.text: I thought the guest host was a big surprise. / No. Surprise. / She's hosted the show 11 times already. / Well, surprise. She's going to do it again.
jokes.setup: The announcement that tonight's guest host is 'the incomparable Sandra Bernhard' is framed as a big surprise.
jokes.punchline: She's hosted 11 times already — the 'surprise' is completely hollow, delivered with flat deadpan as if the word itself has lost meaning.
jokes.explanation: A crisp opener that immediately establishes the show's satirical voice — the hollow showbiz hype machine skewered in two exchanges. The repeated 'surprise' lands because of pure economy and timing. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I thought the guest host was a big surprise. Did you know sandra was going to host the show?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No. Surprise.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: She's hosted the show 11 times already.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, surprise. She's going to do it again.

jokes.text: Here are your answers: You love your job, you love the guests, but most of all, you love Larry. Let's hear it. / We love our job. We love the guests. / I swear to God, I forgot what the last thing was.
jokes.setup: Artie drills the staff on scripted responses to give Gloria Steinem so she doesn't write a hit piece — climaxing in 'most of all, you love Larry.'
jokes.punchline: Someone in the group, almost certainly Hank, has already forgotten 'we love Larry' — the most important and most absurd instruction.
jokes.explanation: Works on two levels: satire of the paranoid, image-conscious world of late-night TV, and character comedy (Hank is perfectly dim enough to forget the one thing that matters most). The line 'I forgot what the last thing was' is perfectly timed and gets funnier knowing who delivers it.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I swear to God, I forgot what the last thing was.

jokes.text: Why? I'm a big supporter of women's rights. / Oh, give me a break.
jokes.setup: Artie warns Hank to stay away from Gloria Steinem. Hank protests that he supports women's rights.
jokes.punchline: Artie's withering 'Oh, give me a break' — a masterclass in flat dismissal — implies he knows exactly what Hank's version of 'supporting women' looks like.
jokes.explanation: Artie's economy is the joke — four words do the work of a paragraph. Character-specific: only Artie can dismiss Hank with this particular brand of weary contempt. Sets up the next joke perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Yeah, Hank. Maybe you could show her your video where you're supporting one woman's rights while another woman is blowing you.

jokes.text: Yeah, Hank. Maybe you could show her your video where you're supporting one woman's rights while another woman is blowing you.
jokes.setup: Hank claims to be a big supporter of women's rights. The staff is skeptical.
jokes.punchline: The existence of a sex tape where Hank's 'support' of women's rights is, graphically and literally, two-tracked.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The comedic concept (a sex tape reframed as feminist activism) is genuinely original, the character specificity is excellent (this could only be Hank), and the double meaning of 'supporting one woman's rights while another woman is blowing you' is structurally elegant — a single sentence that packs a graphic revelation and a conceptual joke simultaneously. Hank's horrified 'How did you find that out?' seals it as a running character indictment.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I also had my penis inverted into a vagina 'cause I figured once I had my eyes done, I'd want to get the whole thing done.

jokes.text: How did you find that out? / You are such an asshole.
jokes.setup: The sex tape joke lands. The room moves on immediately.
jokes.punchline: Hank's panicked 'How did you find that out?' confirms the tape is real, followed immediately by someone calling him an asshole — not for the tape, but for his reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: She's a nurse on ER.

jokes.text: No one knows where I am, right? / No. It's just like you're here at work.
jokes.setup: Larry, supposedly on vacation, calls in to check on things and asks if anyone knows where he is.
jokes.punchline: Artie's response — 'It's just like you're here at work' — perfectly captures the futility of Larry's vacation while deadpanning his obsessive need for control.
jokes.explanation: Economical character-defining joke. Artie's dry response accomplishes two things at once: confirms Larry is incapable of actually vacationing, and delivers his own quiet exasperation. Very Sanders show in its restraint.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: Oh! And yet, I look at you, and I just want to be bald.

jokes.text: You don't think I'm shallow for getting my eyes done, do you? / Hey, whatever makes you happy makes me happy. / I also had my penis inverted into a vagina 'cause I figured once I had my eyes done, I'd want to get the whole thing done.
jokes.setup: Larry fishes for reassurance about his cosmetic eye surgery. Artie gives a reassuring non-answer.
jokes.punchline: Larry casually adds that he also had his penis inverted into a vagina as a logical extension of getting his eyes done — delivered with the same confessional tone as the eye surgery.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The escalation from 'I had my eyes done' to 'I had my penis inverted into a vagina' is a classic misdirection-absurdism combo, but what elevates it is the impeccable logic Larry applies: 'once I had my eyes done, I'd want to get the whole thing done.' The absurd reasoning is delivered with total sincerity, making it funnier than a pure non-sequitur. Character-specific: only Larry's vanity and spiraling anxiety could produce this confession. Nearly 8+ on craft — the structure and originality are genuinely impressive for a phone-call bit.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Hank plays an indian who sits on his own arrow.

jokes.text: Listen, I'm glad to see they haven't removed your sense of humor. / Does it hurt?
jokes.setup: After Larry's absurd gender-reassignment joke, Artie takes a beat to respond.
jokes.punchline: Artie's unfazed 'I'm glad to see they haven't removed your sense of humor' treats the vagina joke as a mere inconvenience, then immediately pivots to practical concern — 'Does it hurt?' — as if the surgery might actually be real.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: I mean, if they want me to be Larry, why don't they just dress me up in one of Larry's purple suits and have me limp over to the desk and act like I have no reason to live?

jokes.text: Well, you know, there's a little, uh... swelling and a little discoloration, but Julianna Margulies says it's gonna go down in a couple of weeks.
jokes.setup: Artie asks if the (eye) surgery hurts. Larry answers about swelling and discoloration — standard recovery.
jokes.punchline: The punchline is Julianna Margulies — a celebrity nurse-character name-drop that recontextualizes 'swelling and discoloration' as potentially referring to the invented penis-inversion, while also riffing on celebrity hypochondria and the absurdity of having ER's nurse as your personal post-op consultant.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: No. I just assumed it was near the freeway when it's called the on-ramp theatre.

jokes.text: There she is. The sexiest, funniest, smartest woman in show business. / Oh! And yet, I look at you, and I just want to be bald.
jokes.setup: Artie heaps lavish praise on Sandra Bernhard — sexiest, funniest, smartest woman in show business.
jokes.punchline: Sandra deflects the compliment by declaring she just wants to be bald when she looks at Artie — a weird, affectionate non-sequitur that captures her singular comedic voice.
jokes.explanation: Very Sandra Bernhard — the response is genuinely strange and personal in a way that only she could deliver. The joke is her personality. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: This guy's addicted to crack, and I have a scene where he can't decide whether to kill himself or to masturbate.

jokes.text: Well, I just dropped by to get my head rubbed.
jokes.setup: Artie and Sandra exchange mutual admiration. Sandra has a new manager in tow and seems to be here for business.
jokes.punchline: Sandra explains she just stopped by to get her head rubbed — a casually bizarre explanation that undercuts any business pretense with pure physical whimsy.
jokes.explanation: Brief but effective. Plays against the setup of a professional arrival and delivers a purely physical, absurd non-explanation. Pure Sandra.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Please come, because if you don't come, I might start doing crack again.

jokes.text: Phil has written another hilarious Dr. Quinn Medicine Woman parody. Hank plays an Indian who sits on his own arrow.
jokes.setup: The writing staff is pitching segment ideas for Sandra's guest-hosting stint.
jokes.punchline: The parody's premise is that Hank plays a Native American who sits on his own arrow — simultaneously making fun of the parody genre, Hank's dignity, and the era's casual political incorrectness with a dark physical-comedy payoff.
jokes.explanation: Works as an absurdist bit-within-a-bit, but the 'Indian' joke is dated and the humor leans on shock more than craft. Earns its place mainly through the specificity of Hank being the one humiliated.

dialogue.line: We love our guests. I love my job.

jokes.text: I go out to do my monologue, and I do this joke that really bombs, so I bring the writer out and I spank him. / Now, that's great stuff.
jokes.setup: Sandra is pitching segment ideas. She describes doing a joke that bombs.
jokes.punchline: Her solution — bringing the writer out and spanking him on air — is absurdly punitive but perfectly on-brand for Sandra's dominatrix-adjacent persona. Artie's 'Now, that's great stuff' is either genuine or the most tired producer affirmation imaginable.
jokes.explanation: Clever bit that works because Sandra is entirely believable doing this. Artie's response adds a second layer — is he genuinely excited or just placating a difficult host?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Women, thank God, are now equal with men, and... although, I gotta tell you, I think men are just a little stronger... but in all other areas, equal. Especially at the crunch. You know... sex time.

jokes.text: They don't want to do anything new on this show. I mean, if they want me to be Larry, why don't they just dress me up in one of Larry's purple suits and have me limp over to the desk and act like I have no reason to live?
jokes.setup: Sandra, alone in the green room, vents about the show's creative conservatism.
jokes.punchline: Her vision of 'being Larry' — purple suits, limping, acting like there's no reason to live — is a savage and affectionate character assassination of Larry Sanders delivered with complete conviction.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. The line 'act like I have no reason to live' is a killer character insight — it's funny precisely because it's TRUE about Larry, and coming from Sandra it's both a roast and an astute critique of the show's own protagonist. The purple suits add a specific, visual absurdist detail. High character integration (Sandra is the only one who could say this with this delivery), and it earns its darkness. One of the episode's best moments.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I was just busily pleasing myself, but now I realize, thanks to you, people like you, it's a 2-way street, and I want to thank you.

jokes.text: Staff robotically responding to Gloria Steinem's arrival: 'We love our guests.' 'We love Larry.' 'I love my job.' — triggered like Pavlovian responses mid-greeting
jokes.setup: Artie drilled the staff with approved responses earlier
jokes.punchline: The staff fire off their scripted lines at random, inappropriate moments in the greeting sequence — completely failing the social interaction they were trained for
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the media training bit. The comedy comes from how badly the rehearsal translates to reality — the responses are technically correct but socially disastrous. The callback structure rewards attentive viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Great ass.

jokes.text: Sandra wants me to book Paul Mooney on the show. He's not a Sanders comic and I don't want to do it.
jokes.setup: Artie discusses Sandra's demands with staff.
jokes.punchline: The phrase 'a Sanders comic' — as if the show has its own comedic taxonomy that Paul Mooney doesn't fit — is both character-revealing (Artie's protectiveness of Larry's brand) and quietly satirical of how late-night TV gatekeeps Black comedians.
jokes.explanation: Understated industry satire. The joke is in what's NOT said — the implication of what 'a Sanders comic' means racially is left entirely to the viewer. Smart but not perfectly executed.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Let me guess. Are you pissed because you didn't get to host again?

jokes.text: What's this serious piece about, Phil? / Well, it's about a writer who writes for late-night television. / Oh, it's about you! / No, no. I knew you'd say that. It's loosely based on me, but it's very dark. This guy's addicted to crack, and I have a scene where he can't decide whether to kill himself or to masturbate.
jokes.setup: Phil insists his serious play is not about him. It's loosely based on him. It's very dark.
jokes.punchline: The play's pivotal dramatic scene: a man who can't decide whether to kill himself or masturbate. The escalating darkness of each detail Phil adds, delivered with artistic seriousness, is perfectly paced.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The pivot from 'it's not about me' to 'loosely based on me' to 'he's addicted to crack' to 'can't decide whether to kill himself or masturbate' is perfect escalation — each revelation funnier than the last. The structure is immaculate, character integration is high (Phil's creative self-delusion and grandiosity are central to his character), and the final image is both horrifying and hilarious. Genuinely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'll have Paula give you the phone number of my buddy oliver stone.

jokes.text: Brian's tour-guide line about the plants: 'Artie takes care of them all by himself. Isn't that cute? Very versatile guy.' — desperately filling silence while managing Steinem
jokes.setup: Brian is tasked with giving Gloria Steinem a 'grand tour' to keep her away from the staff
jokes.punchline: The 'grand tour' consists of pointing out the plants and marveling at Artie's horticultural versatility
jokes.explanation: A solid cringe beat — Brian is clearly out of his depth trying to entertain one of America's most prominent feminist intellectuals with plant trivia. The 'very versatile guy' pivot is the sad flourish. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I tell you there's a conspiracy, and you tell me to put on makeup, but then she walks in, tells you, and you're all ears. It's always about you, isn't it?

jokes.text: Oh, how can you deny that's about you?
jokes.setup: Phil insists the character addicted to crack who can't decide between suicide and masturbation is NOT him.
jokes.punchline: The inevitable reaction — 'how can you deny that's about you?' — is the comedy of watching someone maintain a delusion in real time.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: Who knew I was gonna come floating out here in a pair of manolo blahnik lucite high heels... that I happened to borrow from Larry.

jokes.text: Please come, because if you don't come, I might start doing crack again.
jokes.setup: Phil is begging coworkers to attend his play.
jokes.punchline: His incentive for attendance: if they don't come, he might relapse into crack cocaine. The word 'again' is doing enormous work.
jokes.explanation: The word 'again' turns this from a joke into a character revelation. The sentence does three things at once: confirms the play IS autobiographical, reveals Phil has a crack history, and weaponizes sympathy as a ticket-sale strategy. Maximum economy. One of the best line deliveries in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: but I'm just here to kind of abuse you again and tell you that's what I do. Nyah! No.

jokes.text: OK, OK. If it's Friday, I'll go. / We'll all go. I'll rent a plane.
jokes.setup: Phil has successfully guilted the staff into attending his play 45 minutes away in Hawthorne.
jokes.punchline: Someone offers to rent a plane to get to a tiny fringe theater in Hawthorne — an absurdly outsized solution to a minor inconvenience, delivered as if it's a perfectly proportionate offer.
jokes.explanation: Mild escalation joke — the absurdity of a plane for Hawthorne works but isn't particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: The managers usually stay in the green room by the shrimp plate.

jokes.text: Hank, they need to see you in wardrobe. / Just one minute. / They need to see you in wardrobe. / And I'll tell you why. Women, thank God, are now equal with men, and... although, I gotta tell you, I think men are just a little stronger... [long pause]
jokes.setup: Artie has warned Hank to stay away from Gloria Steinem. Hank launches into a speech about women's rights directly to Steinem, while Beverly frantically tries to extract him.
jokes.punchline: Hank's feminist speech immediately betrays itself — 'I think men are just a little stronger' — while Beverly's increasingly desperate wardrobe interventions go completely unheeded. The pause after 'stronger' is the cringe peak.
jokes.explanation: Sustained cringe sequence built on everything we know about Hank. The joke is that he genuinely believes he's an ally while systematically undercutting every feminist position he tries to articulate. Beverly's repeated wardrobe interventions add escalating desperation. The awkward pause after 'men are just a little stronger' is the comedy of watching someone realize, mid-sentence, they've said something terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: All right? Now, I'm not saying that I want to see Gary on the cover of allure, but I can bet one thing. Naomi campbell wouldn't have dragged her tired ass over to my house to fix my hot water heater, OK?

jokes.text: ...but in all other areas, equal. Especially at the crunch. You know... sex time.
jokes.setup: Hank is recovering from saying men are 'just a little stronger' — backpedaling to reassure Steinem of his feminist credentials.
jokes.punchline: 'Especially at the crunch. You know... sex time.' Hank's attempt to compliment women's sexual equality lands as the most inadvertently inappropriate thing he could say to Gloria Steinem.
jokes.explanation: The apex of the Hank/Steinem cringe sequence. 'Sex time' is one of the funniest two-word punchlines in the episode — it's exactly the kind of thing Hank would say, the exact wrong thing to say to this particular person, and the pause before it ('You know...') makes it land even harder. Character integration is nearly perfect: this joke exists nowhere else in television except in Hank Kingsley's mouth. Comparable to the snip-snap calibration anchor in terms of character-specific comic humiliation.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: I know you got this thing set up to hide the bolts in Larry's neck.

jokes.text: Before, I just never even considered... / pleasing another woman?
jokes.setup: Hank trails off — apparently trying to articulate that he never previously considered women's perspectives.
jokes.punchline: Steinem completes his sentence with '...pleasing another woman?' — a perfectly placed, devastating completion that reveals her awareness of exactly what kind of man Hank is.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed. The joke hinges on Steinem — a real feminist icon — appearing to reference Hank's sex tape (which the audience knows about) while completing his sentence. The economy is exceptional: two words ('pleasing another woman') do the work of a callback, a character revelation, and a feminist rebuttal simultaneously. Steinem's deadpan delivery (implied) makes it cut deeper. This is elite Larry Sanders comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Rob
dialogue.line: That's a rabbit.

jokes.text: Um... you know, it's getting late. I think I should make a phone call in the dressing room.
jokes.setup: After Hank thanks Steinem for making him realize it's a 'two-way street' and he wants to please people — following the 'sex time' moment.
jokes.punchline: Steinem's polite, utterly transparent escape — 'I think I should make a phone call in the dressing room' — is the comedy of someone with too much dignity to actually respond to what just happened.
jokes.explanation: The polite exit as punchline. Works because Steinem is a real person playing along with the joke — her retreat is the most eloquent possible response to Hank's feminist monologue. The understated dignity of 'I think I should make a phone call' is pitch-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Rob
dialogue.line: That's the rectum.

jokes.text: Great ass.
jokes.setup: Gloria Steinem has just left to make a 'phone call' after Hank's disastrous feminist monologue.
jokes.punchline: Hank watches her go and says 'Great ass.' — confirming in two words that he has absorbed absolutely nothing.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the great sitcom button lines. Two words. No setup needed — the entire Hank/Steinem sequence IS the setup. After multiple failed attempts to demonstrate his feminist credentials (including 'sex time'), Hank reduces Gloria Steinem to a body part assessment. The economy is flawless: ten words of feminist posturing punctuated by two words of total self-indictment. The joke also works as a callback to the sex tape — everything Hank said was hollow and now we see why. Character integration is as high as it gets: this is the Platonic ideal of a Hank Kingsley line.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: Hank, want to get in here and do a quick exam?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Sandra
dialogue.line: Just kidding.

jokes.text: You know, the show is starting to creak. Sandra skews to a much younger audience than Larry does. They should grab her before Fox does. / Or ABC.
jokes.setup: Ellen is making a business case for Sandra taking over the show.
jokes.punchline: Artie adds 'Or ABC' in a flat, utterly unenthusiastic tone — ambiguous as to whether he's agreeing sardonically, playing along with contempt, or genuinely noting the threat. The ambiguity is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Understated industry comedy. Artie's 'Or ABC' is either dry capitulation or dry contempt — the show trusts the viewer to read Rip Torn's delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, that depends on what day of the week it is. I believe on Monday it's Manhattan clam chowder.

jokes.text: Sandra Bernhard is trying to take over the show. / Let me guess. Are you pissed because you didn't get to host again? / No, no, I'm not pissed.
jokes.setup: Hank bursts in claiming Sandra is conspiring to take the show. Artie immediately diagnoses the real issue.
jokes.punchline: Artie guesses correctly — Hank's outrage is really jealousy about not getting to host — and Hank denies it too quickly.
jokes.explanation: Classic character comedy — Artie as the only adult in the room, instantly seeing through Hank's self-deception. Functional and character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Ellen
dialogue.line: I think we should give Hank the next 2 weeks off. What do you think?

jokes.text: OK. Here's my advice. Go put on some makeup. You'll feel better. And afterwards, if you still think there's a conspiracy, I'll have Paula give you the phone number of my buddy Oliver Stone.
jokes.setup: Hank is convinced there's a conspiracy against Larry involving Sandra's manager.
jokes.punchline: Artie's advice: (1) put on some makeup, (2) if you still think there's a conspiracy, call Oliver Stone. The dismissiveness is total — he treats Hank's paranoia as a mood disorder addressable by cosmetics, with Oliver Stone as the emergency contact for genuine conspiracy theorists.
jokes.explanation: Very strong Artie line. The Oliver Stone reference is a period-perfect (1995) pop culture joke with genuine craft — it's not just a name-drop but a logical extension of Hank's paranoia. The makeup suggestion adds a layer of casual emasculation. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Julianna
dialogue.line: You know what, Larry? I can't check the swelling if you don't let me touch it.

jokes.text: I tell you there's a conspiracy, and you tell me to put on makeup, but then she walks in, tells you, and you're all ears. / It's always about you, isn't it?
jokes.setup: Beverly confirms Hank's conspiracy theory — Sandra's manager IS conspiring — and Artie immediately takes it seriously. Hank is furious at the double standard.
jokes.punchline: Artie dismisses Hank's legitimate grievance with 'It's always about you, isn't it?' — which is rich, given that Artie just did exactly what Hank accused him of doing.
jokes.explanation: Artie turns hypocrisy into a power move by deflecting with a meta-accusation of narcissism. The irony is rich and character-specific. Good payoff to the conspiracy subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Julianna
dialogue.line: You start tightening up your face, it just makes your ass look enormous.

jokes.text: Who knew I was gonna come floating out here in a pair of Manolo Blahnik lucite high heels... that I happened to borrow from Larry.
jokes.setup: Sandra begins her on-air monologue as guest host.
jokes.punchline: She's wearing Larry's Manolo Blahnik lucite heels — establishing both Larry's vanity/fashion choices and Sandra's effortless appropriation of his identity.
jokes.explanation: Strong opener for the on-air segment. The Manolo Blahniks being Larry's is a character joke that works on the real-life Larry (Shandling's known vanity) and the fictional Larry (the purple suits callback). Marks the blurring of guest host and actual host.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I think it's learned how to read.

jokes.text: Once I wear them, I kind of just go, 'uhh! I can't wear that again.' I know how most of you women feel about that, you know. I know you like to think that you can possibly wear something once and never wear it again, but I'm just here to kind of abuse you again and tell you that's what I do. Nyah! No.
jokes.setup: Sandra discusses her fashion habits — wearing something once and discarding it.
jokes.punchline: She acknowledges the class gap between her disposable fashion habits and the audience ('barely scraping it together to go to Lerner's') — but frames it as 'abusing' them rather than apologizing. The 'Nyah! No' seals it as performative provocation.
jokes.explanation: Solid Sandra Bernhard persona comedy — the deliberate provocation of flaunting wealth while acknowledging the audience's relative poverty is very on-brand. Slightly bloated in execution; could be tighter.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Do you know if he's gay? Because I'd blow him.

jokes.text: The managers usually stay in the green room by the shrimp plate. / I don't eat shellfish. / There's also some very fine old rotting cheese there.
jokes.setup: Ellen has come onto the set — out of her lane as a manager. Sandra calls her out by directing her to the shrimp plate.
jokes.punchline: Ellen says she doesn't eat shellfish. Sandra pivots immediately to 'some very fine old rotting cheese' — the comic escalation of the insult from shrimp to rotten cheese while maintaining complete pleasantness.
jokes.explanation: Very Sandra. The pivot from shrimp to rotting cheese is elegant — the insult escalates as the options degrade, but Sandra delivers it as if she's being genuinely helpful. Good character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: You will? You'll get down on your knees and you'll put his penis in your mouth?

jokes.text: I'm not saying that I want to see Gary on the cover of Allure, but I can bet one thing. Naomi Campbell wouldn't have dragged her tired ass over to my house to fix my hot water heater, OK?
jokes.setup: Sandra argues plumbers are more valuable than supermodels.
jokes.punchline: The image of Naomi Campbell dragging her 'tired ass' over to fix a hot water heater — the juxtaposition of supermodel glamour and plumbing emergency — is the joke. Clean and well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Well, since you put it that way, I guess it's not so appealing.

jokes.text: Now, one of your essays is 'If Men Could Menstruate.' Have I said that right? It's such a hard word, even though I am a woman and I do...
jokes.setup: Sandra introduces Steinem's essay on air with the title 'If Men Could Menstruate.'
jokes.punchline: Sandra stumbles on the word 'menstruate' — 'It's such a hard word, even though I am a woman and I do...' — creating a perfect awkward self-interruption, the comedy of a very confident person suddenly flustered by biology.
jokes.explanation: The comedy of someone who handles every outrageous topic with aplomb being undone by a clinical word she should have no problem saying. The unfinished 'even though I am a woman and I do...' is perfectly timed — what follows is silence where a sentence should be.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: She's evil and fat and she wants your show.

jokes.text: They would brag about how long and how much... / I know you got this thing set up to hide the bolts in Larry's neck.
jokes.setup: Steinem is explaining her 'If Men Could Menstruate' essay — men would brag about duration and volume.
jokes.punchline: Sandra interrupts mid-sentence with a meta joke about the show's lighting hiding 'the bolts in Larry's neck' — a Frankenstein reference to Larry's cosmetic surgery, breaking the interview to make a joke about the absent host.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Maybe Mark fuhrman planted it.

jokes.text: Can't you dump a little more light in there? You got it, Igor.
jokes.setup: Sandra has just made the 'bolts in Larry's neck' comment.
jokes.punchline: She calls the lighting technician 'Igor' — fully committing to the Frankenstein bit — while directing the show's own lighting crew on air.

dialogue.line: Friday is 'mystery meat.'

jokes.text: Now, she seems to be a little big through the middle. / Well, that's a... that's a rabbit. It's a rabbit.
jokes.setup: Sandra is examining an albino Burmese python on the desk, noting it looks 'a little big through the middle.'
jokes.punchline: The snake expert confirms: there's a rabbit inside the snake. A contained, horrifying revelation delivered matter-of-factly.
jokes.explanation: Classic late-night snake segment subverted. The flat delivery of 'that's a rabbit' makes it funnier than any shocked reaction would. The dark implication (the rabbit is digesting inside the snake) is left understated.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I've had no surgery at all.

jokes.text: Now, is this the kind of snake that will wr... oh, what is that there? What's that hole there? / That's the rectum. / Hank, want to get in here and do a quick exam?
jokes.setup: Sandra's sentence is interrupted by noticing something anatomically notable on the snake.
jokes.punchline: The snake's rectum is identified, and Sandra immediately invites Hank to 'do a quick exam' — a joke about both the snake's anatomy and what Hank might enjoy.
jokes.explanation: The invitation to Hank is the joke — the implication is either that Hank is associated with snakes/rectums or that Sandra enjoys tormenting him. Either way, it's earned by the preceding Hank sequences.

dialogue.line: In the middle of the second act, a car flew off the freeway, crashed through the wall of the theater, and took out the first couple of rows. Fortunately, no one was there.

jokes.text: Look at her eyes. Look at her eyes. They're so... / No, no, no, no. / You said, look at 'em. / I know. I'm looking. Her eyes are really incred... / Hank, look into her eyes. / I got it. I'm fine right here.
jokes.setup: Sandra encourages Hank to look at the python's eyes. Hank is terrified of the snake.
jokes.punchline: Hank's retreat — 'I got it. I'm fine right here' — while Sandra persistently draws him toward a large python is sustained discomfort comedy, the audience watching a man lose ground incrementally.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — the camera presumably showing Hank inching away while pretending to be fine. Physical comedy inferred from dialogue.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Oh, he's on crack.

jokes.text: Sandra keeps telling Hank to look into the snake's eyes — 'She's kind of an enchantress, Hank. I think you might get into her.' Hank is terrified and refuses.
jokes.setup: Sandra is enthusiastically engaging with the snake; she tries to get Hank involved
jokes.punchline: Hank's mounting panic — 'I got it. I'm fine right here.' — contrasted with Sandra's increasingly suggestive insistence ('you could have a moment with Annabelle')
jokes.explanation: The snake-seduction angle works as a sustained cringe bit — Sandra implying that a man and a giant python could 'have a moment' while Hank retreats is a good sustained awkward beat. The 'Annabelle' name-personalization is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Network Executive
dialogue.line: Um... 3-8. But sandra got a younger demographic.

jokes.text: Hank gave her nothing out there. What's up his ass? / Well, that depends on what day of the week it is. I believe on Monday it's Manhattan clam chowder.
jokes.setup: Ellen complains about Hank's poor performance during the snake segment.
jokes.punchline: Artie's response — what's up Hank's ass depends on the day, and Monday is Manhattan clam chowder — is a dark, bizarre escalation that implies both anal fixation and a detailed knowledge of Hank's intimate life that no one should have.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes. The structure is perfect — Ellen's idiomatic 'what's up his ass?' invites the literal interpretation, and Artie takes it somewhere nobody expected: a weekly schedule, with the specificity of 'Manhattan clam chowder' on Mondays. The joke is funnier for being delivered by Artie as if it's common knowledge. The specificity of the soup variety elevates this from crude to genuinely inventive. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor example — sharp, unexpected, quotable, perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I was just saying to my dog Bob packwood, I said...

jokes.text: Would you shut your mouth just one second, Ellen, my dear? / Maybe it's you that's causing my back pain.
jokes.setup: Sandra throws her back out and Artie is hovering; Ellen suggests giving Hank two weeks off.
jokes.punchline: Sandra, in pain, turns on Ellen with 'Maybe it's you that's causing my back pain' — a psychosomatic accusation that is both funny and tells us everything about their dynamic.
jokes.explanation: Moderate character beat. The psychosomatic accusation is a bit lazy but works in the moment because it characterizes the Sandra/Ellen relationship quickly.

dialogue.line: evidently hoping to take another whack at it.

jokes.text: You remember when you sit out there, you're sitting in Larry's chair. And you got it? / I'm sitting behind that desk for the next 2 weeks. / Well, I'll be sitting right next to you. / Oh, it's going to be a big fucking party, isn't it?
jokes.setup: There's a tense standoff between Artie, Sandra (who just told him off), and Hank.
jokes.punchline: Hank's chipper 'Well, I'll be sitting right next to you' — offered as a peace offering — is met with Sandra's devastating 'Oh, it's going to be a big fucking party, isn't it?' — the comedy of someone trying to make peace with a land mine.
jokes.explanation: Sandra's 'big fucking party' is a perfect button on a tense scene — the sarcasm is delivered at the exact right temperature.

dialogue.speaker: Network Executive
dialogue.line: Maybe 8 years of Larry is enough.

jokes.text: Would you not touch me while I'm on the phone, please? / Hello? / I can't check the swelling if you don't let me touch it. / I'm sorry. I just... I can't concentrate when you're touching me.
jokes.setup: Larry is on the phone with Artie reporting on the show. Someone (Julianna Margulies) is apparently touching him.
jokes.punchline: The conversation implies Margulies is checking his post-surgical 'swelling' while he's trying to manage his TV show, and he can't concentrate — which callbacks his invented penis-inversion joke while also being genuinely funny as a celebrity-adjacent awkward moment.

jokes.text: Oh, God. Look at you. / Do I look good? I look good, huh? / See, this is why I would never have plastic surgery. / Oh, come on. You had your eyes done. / Oh, please. I did not. / You start tightening up your face, it just makes your ass look enormous.
jokes.setup: Larry, post-surgery, fishes for compliments from Beverly about his appearance. Beverly denies having had work done herself.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's logic: tightening your face just makes your ass look enormous. A perfectly absurd cosmetic reasoning that both dismisses Larry's surgery and reveals Beverly's own beauty anxiety.
jokes.explanation: The logic is air-tight within its own absurdity: if your face gets tighter, by contrast your ass looks bigger. It's simultaneously a vanity joke about Beverly, a dig at Larry's surgery, and a commentary on Hollywood appearance anxiety. Quotable and specific.

jokes.text: I think it's learned how to read.
jokes.setup: Artie throws his back out and comments that it seems to happen at the worst moments — specifically when there's a threatening L.A. Times article about Larry.
jokes.punchline: 'I think it's learned how to read' — Artie's back has developed literacy. A perfect deadpan absurdist one-liner.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best single-line joke. Perfect economy — six words that are completely unexpected, perfectly logical within their absurdity (the back hurts when stress is high, therefore the back has learned to read stress indicators), and delivered by Rip Torn in a way that makes it sound like a reasonable medical diagnosis. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in terms of economy and originality. The brevity is everything — this is what maximum funny per word looks like.

jokes.text: Larry must not see this article. / Oh, I'm way ahead of you. I'm on my way to his house. / Oh, let's go. I'll... take my car. / I'll drive. We'll use the siren.
jokes.setup: Beverly and Artie conspire to keep a damaging L.A. Times article from Larry.
jokes.punchline: 'We'll use the siren.' Artie apparently has a siren on his car — a detail so specific and absurd that it recontextualizes Artie as someone who has prepared for exactly this kind of emergency.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'I'll take my car' to 'I'll drive. We'll use the siren' is perfect — Artie has a siren, and of course he does. It's completely Artie. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Oh! You know, if this guy gives me a good review, I'll pay him a thousand bucks. Do you know if he's gay? Because I'd blow him. / Phil, that's not funny. / No. I'm not being funny. I mean, if he gives me a good review, I will blow him.
jokes.setup: Phil learns the L.A. Weekly reviewer is coming to his play and wants a good review.
jokes.punchline: Phil escalates from $1,000 bribe to sexual favor, and when corrected ('that's not funny'), he insists he's being completely sincere — the comedy of someone whose desperation has erased the line between joke and genuine offer.
jokes.explanation: Phil's earnestness is the engine of the joke. Brian saying 'that's not funny' followed by Phil's 'I'm not being funny' creates a beautiful Abbot and Costello-style miscommunication — they're both right, but for different reasons.

jokes.text: You will? You'll get down on your knees and you'll put his penis in your mouth? / Well, since you put it that way, I guess it's not so appealing. / Yeah, exactly. Huh? Huh?
jokes.setup: Phil has earnestly declared he would blow a reviewer for a good review. Brian pushes back by spelling out exactly what that means.
jokes.punchline: Brian's clinical description — 'get down on your knees and put his penis in your mouth' — forces Phil to confront the literal reality of his offer. Phil's 'since you put it that way' is the comedy of euphemism punctured by bluntness.

jokes.text: Who the fuck planted this? / It's Sandra's manager, Larry. She's evil and fat and she wants your show.
jokes.setup: Larry has arrived, presumably having seen the L.A. Times article despite Artie and Beverly's efforts.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's description of Ellen Boyd: 'She's evil and fat and she wants your show.' The 'fat' in the middle is the joke — Beverly's insult list includes a moral judgment, a physical judgment, and a professional threat, treating them as equal concerns.
jokes.explanation: The comic logic of 'evil and fat and she wants your show' — listing body type as if it's equivalent evidence of villainy — is both funny and a sharp satirical note about Hollywood values.

jokes.text: Larry arrives at the studio in sunglasses, paranoid. Beverly: 'Who the fuck planted this?' — apparently about paparazzi or press.
jokes.setup: Larry tries to arrive at the studio secretly while on 'vacation'
jokes.punchline: The chaos of his arrival — sunglasses, jacket management, someone shouting about who planted something — undercuts the supposed secret recovery
jokes.explanation: The arrival sequence is more plot than comedy — it establishes that Larry is back. Beverly's 'evil and fat' line about Ellen is a bit much. Functional transitional scene.

jokes.text: Maybe Mark Fuhrman planted it. / Ha ha ha! Is he managing you now?
jokes.setup: Larry confronts Sandra about whether her manager planted the L.A. Times article. Sandra deflects.
jokes.punchline: Sandra invokes Mark Fuhrman — the disgraced LAPD detective from the O.J. trial, then very much in the news — as an alternative planting suspect. Larry's callback 'Is he managing you now?' extends the joke perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Sharp topical joke — the O.J. trial was live news in 1995, and Fuhrman was THE symbol of evidence planting. The joke works because it's the exact right reference for 'planted' evidence in L.A., and it's delivered by Sandra with perfect timing. Larry's follow-up is a solid button.

jokes.text: So, the plan is... we're going to serve America a talk-show smorgasbord. Jon Stewart tonight, Rosie O'Donnell the next, and then Dennis Miller. / What's Friday? / Friday is 'mystery meat.'
jokes.setup: The network executive explains the guest-host rotation to fill Larry's absence.
jokes.punchline: 'Mystery meat' for Friday — the network has already categorized its own programming as a cafeteria food metaphor, and Friday's host is whoever's left at the bottom of the barrel.
jokes.explanation: The smorgasbord metaphor is well-executed showbiz satire — the network treating human talent as cafeteria options, with 'mystery meat' as the dark endpoint. Crisp and well-structured.

jokes.text: You look as fresh as springtime, like the apple-cheeked boy who walked through this curtain 8 years ago. / Well, and keeping these apples in my cheeks is killing me, by the way.
jokes.setup: Sid flatters Larry with a lavish compliment about looking 'fresh as springtime' with 'apple-cheeked' youth.
jokes.punchline: Larry's deadpan: 'keeping these apples in my cheeks is killing me, by the way' — a perfect double entendre (literal cheek fillers and the effort of performing the Larry Sanders persona), delivered as an aside.
jokes.explanation: Very strong. The line works on two levels: literally (cheek fillers hurt) and metaphorically (performing youthful charm for 8 years is exhausting). It's also a callback to the surgery thread, a character revelation, and a meta-comment on Shandling's own performing persona. Character integration is exceptionally high — this joke is inseparable from Larry as a character.

jokes.text: Shouldn't you be doing the warmup? / You see? I can't get this from anybody else. This... this right here. This is our relationship.
jokes.setup: Hank is effusively glad to see Larry back. Larry responds by asking if Hank should be doing warmup — a mild but clear dismissal.
jokes.punchline: Hank's response — 'I can't get this from anybody else. This is our relationship' — interprets Larry's brush-off as intimate connection. Hank has decided that Larry ignoring him IS their relationship, and he's grateful for it.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most character-rich jokes. The joke is that Hank is right — this IS their relationship — and it's both sad and hilarious. Larry's dismissiveness IS the intimacy. The line 'I can't get this from anybody else' reframes Larry's contempt as a love language. Very high character integration: this could only be Hank Kingsley, the man who mistakes crumbs for feasts.

jokes.text: Listen, I've gotta get those tickets to Phil's play. / Oh, it closed on Friday. / I thought it opened on Friday. / Well, the oddest thing happened. In the middle of the second act, a car flew off the freeway, crashed through the wall of the theater, and took out the first couple of rows. / Fortunately, no one was there. / Well, he sure seems to be handling it pretty well. / Oh, he's on crack.
jokes.setup: Larry mentions getting tickets to Phil's play — which just opened on Friday.
jokes.punchline: The play opened and closed on the same night when a car flew off a freeway and crashed through the theater wall. Fortunately no one was there. Phil is handling it well because he's back on crack.
jokes.explanation: The episode's masterpiece joke and one of the finest callback payoffs in the series. Every element of the setup pays off simultaneously: the On-Ramp Theatre (near the freeway — the name was the prediction), the play closing before it could run, Phil's crack threat from earlier, and the glorious detail 'fortunately, no one was there.' Artie's delivery of each revelation as if reading from a dull memo is the technique — the absurdity escalates while the emotional register stays flat. The car-flying-off-the-freeway callback to the theater's name (On-Ramp) is the comedy architecture working at its very best. 'Oh, he's on crack' as the final button is earned because Phil threatened it would happen. Near-perfect structure, extraordinary economy, deeply character-specific (only Phil's life could produce this outcome). This is what a 9+ looks like.

jokes.text: Beverly explains the play closed because 'in the middle of the second act, a car flew off the freeway, crashed through the wall of the theater, and took out the first couple of rows. Fortunately, no one was there.'
jokes.setup: Artie asks why the play closed on opening night
jokes.punchline: A car flew off the freeway and crashed through the theater wall — but 'fortunately, no one was there' — the accident is less damaging than the lack of audience
jokes.explanation: The episode's second-best joke and a masterclass in payoff. The 'On-Ramp Theatre' name-joke from earlier (Joke #13) pays off brilliantly here: a car literally flies off a freeway and into the theater because of course it does — it's a theater called 'On-Ramp' near a highway. But the real genius is 'fortunately, no one was there' — the absence of an audience is presented as more fortunate than avoiding the car crash. Two simultaneous punchlines: the physical comedy and the brutal comment on the play's failure. Near-perfect construction.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Well, he sure seems to be handling it pretty well.' Beverly: 'Oh, he's on crack.'
jokes.setup: They observe that Phil is handling the catastrophic failure of his play serenely
jokes.punchline: He's on crack — confirming that his play's autobiographical crack addiction is not entirely fictional
jokes.explanation: Three words. 'Oh, he's on crack.' Maximum economy, maximum payoff. This joke pays off: (1) Phil's promise to do crack again if no one came to his play (they didn't), (2) the autobiographical nature of the crack character he denied writing, and (3) explains his equanimity about the disaster. The callback chain is three jokes deep. It could have been played as a dramatic beat and instead it's the funniest possible punchline, delivered as a throwaway. Calibrating against anchors: this approaches the top tier of the episode.

jokes.text: What were Sandra Bernhard's ratings? / Um... 3-8. / Mm-hmm. And Larry's? / 3-8. / But Sandra got a younger demographic.
jokes.setup: Larry has returned to work and is now checking the ratings from Sandra's guest-hosting week.
jokes.punchline: Sandra got the exact same ratings as Larry, but the consolation prize is 'she got a younger demographic' — the showbiz equivalent of 'but other than that, Mrs. Lincoln.' Larry's silent processing of this is the real punchline.
jokes.explanation: Devastatingly well-structured. The information lands in steps — same ratings, but younger demo — that peel back the onion of Larry's irrelevance. The joke is industry satire at its sharpest: Larry came back for nothing, and everyone in the room knows it, and they're all pretending the 'younger demo' is a consolation. Larry's reaction (implied: silent horror) is the real punchline.

jokes.text: Please. Even though I was off for a week, do not pity me. Don't force your laughs.
jokes.setup: Larry is doing his monologue, aware of the ratings situation.
jokes.punchline: Larry acknowledges to his studio audience that they might be forcing laughs out of pity — a meta-moment where Larry's insecurity becomes a direct address that is itself the joke.
jokes.explanation: Strong Larry character moment — his insecurity makes him pre-emptively undercut the audience's sympathy, which is itself a very Larry thing to do. The meta awareness is true to character.

jokes.text: Speaking of which, they just said... they discovered that sexual harassment is now evident in animals. / I was just saying to my dog Bob Packwood, I said...
jokes.setup: Larry transitions to his monologue material about a discovery regarding sexual harassment in the animal kingdom.
jokes.punchline: His dog is named Bob Packwood — after the U.S. Senator who had resigned over sexual harassment allegations just weeks before the episode aired. Naming a dog after the country's most notorious workplace harasser is a sharp, economy-packed political joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic monologue construction — the setup about 'sexual harassment in animals' primes you, and then the punchline is just a proper noun: Bob Packwood. The dog-naming as political punchline is elegant. Period-specific topical comedy that holds up structurally.

jokes.text: If a guest host can get the same ratings as Larry, just imagine how much money we could save not having to pay Larry's salary. / What are you saying? / We should get rid of Larry and replace him with Sandra? / It doesn't have to be Sandra. It could be Jon Stewart, Rosie O'Donnell... John Wayne Bobbitt...
jokes.setup: The network executive begins making the financial case for replacing Larry.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from Jon Stewart and Rosie O'Donnell to John Wayne Bobbitt — the man whose penis was famously cut off — as potential late-night replacements for Larry. The show treats Bobbitt as a legitimate hosting candidate.
jokes.explanation: The network exec treating Bobbitt as a legitimate hosting option is the joke — pure showbiz satire about how celebrity notoriety is fungible currency in television.

jokes.text: John Wayne Bobbitt, you would have thought that story would have been over a year and a half ago, but he has just, evidently, shown up... at the beauty salon where his wife works, with flowers, evidently hoping to take another whack at it.
jokes.setup: Larry introduces the Bobbitt reference in his monologue — noting Bobbitt has appeared at his ex-wife's salon with flowers.
jokes.punchline: 'Hoping to take another whack at it' — the double entendre (reconciliation attempt vs. the original incident of penile severing) is the joke. 'Whack' is doing enormous work in a single syllable.

jokes.text: Larry does have a certain charm. Hmm. / Maybe 8 years of Larry is enough.
jokes.setup: Two network executives observe Larry doing his monologue, openly discussing whether to replace him as he performs.
jokes.punchline: 'Maybe 8 years of Larry is enough' — the show's final line, a bleak, perfectly timed button that is both an industry joke (networks' callousness toward talent) and a meta-comment on the show's own longevity questions.
jokes.explanation: A devastating episode-closing line. The image of Larry performing while network executives openly discuss his obsolescence captures everything the show is about — the precarity of showbiz, the dehumanization of talent, and Larry's blissful unawareness. The economy is superb: eight words that close the episode's thematic arc. Earns its high score because it functions simultaneously as a punchline and as a statement of the show's entire thesis.

tmdb_overview: Larry takes a vacation to recover from plastic surgery leaving Sandra Bernhard to fill in as the show host. But her manager sends shock waves through the office with her pushy ways.
